---
name: lumen-adapter-accumulator-real-data-gaps
description: "Inventory of Lumen adapter/accumulator design decisions made from inference rather than verified real session data, discovered 2026-08-20 -- needed before any further Lumen spec/implementation work."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 36644eef-36d9-4e53-b672-5ddcebfc54f0
  modified: 2026-08-20T22:12:18.276Z
---

On 2026-08-20, after believing Lumen's `SPEC-002-SESSION`/`SPEC-005-ANALYSIS` work was solid (green tests, adversarial-reviewed plan), a user question ("what does Kimi/Qwen use for session info?") led to checking real session files on disk instead of guessing, which cascaded into finding that several "verified" designs were never checked against real data — only checked for internal self-consistency (code matches its own spec criterion), which is a much weaker claim.

## Confirmed wrong (not just narrow) -- needs a real rewrite, not a patch

- **`CodexAdapter`** (`crates/lumen-session/src/adapters/codex.rs`): built on an assumed raw-OpenAI-Chat-Completions-API shape (`choices[].message`, `usage.prompt_tokens`). Real Codex CLI rollout files (`~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl`) use a completely different envelope format: `{timestamp, ordinal, type, payload}`, with `event_msg/token_count` for cumulative usage and `response_item/message` + `custom_tool_call`/`custom_tool_call_output` (or a second, distinct `function_call`/`function_call_output` pair) for turns. Verified directly against a real, live local session file.
- **`OpenCodeAdapter`**: built on an assumed `action`/`observation`/`source` JSONL shape with **zero basis in any real OpenCode version, ever** (confirmed via CodeBurn's own source comment). Real OpenCode has exactly two generations: legacy file-based JSON (`storage/session|message|part/*.json`, pre-1.1) and current SQLite (`session`/`message`/`part` tables, verified directly via `sqlite3` on a real local `opencode.db`). Both share one `role`/`type` shape neither matches Lumen's assumption.
- **`HookActivityAccumulator`** (`crates/lumen-analysis/src/accumulators/hook_activity.rs`, spec'd as `CRIT-LUMEN-139`/`140`): field names (`hookEventName`, `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`, `permissionDecision`) were inferred from "general knowledge," never checked against a real hook-execution record. ## External research wave, part 2, 2026-08-20 (LangSmith evaluation-concepts/observability, IBM/TDS/Elastic/Splunk LLM-observability overviews, real OTel GenAI semantic conventions, academic literature)

- **The single most important finding of the whole research wave: both `otel_request_ids` (on `CanonicalTranscript`) and `otel_span_id` (on `CanonicalToolResult`) are structurally wrong relative to the real, authoritative spec** (`github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`), not just unpopulated placeholders. The real correlator is `gen_ai.conversation.id` -- one singular ID per *session*, attached to many per-call spans -- not a small list collected at the transcript level. `gen_ai.response.id` is per-call and would belong on `CanonicalTurn`, not the transcript. `otel_span_id` conflates a real distributed-tracing span ID (16-hex protocol identifier -- a materially bigger, currently-unscoped feature) with what `SpanMappingAccumulator` actually tries to do (correlate a tool call to something), which already has an answer: `gen_ai.tool.call.id` is functionally identical to Lumen's *existing* `call_id` field -- `SpanMappingAccumulator` may not need to exist as currently conceived. One good side-effect: `gen_ai.agent.name`/`gen_ai.workflow.name` are a clean, ecosystem-agnostic answer to the `AttributionSource::{Plugin,Skill}` taxonomy problem (ties two separate gaps into one fix), and `gen_ai.conversation.compacted` is a standard way to represent what Lumen's PreCompact snapshot-merge logic already does internally. Tool calls are a separate span type from inference calls in the real spec; MCP tool calls have their own dedicated conventions file.
- **Industry-standard LLM observability pillars** (synthesized from IBM/TDS/Elastic/Splunk, IBM's own page 403-blocked): functional/performance (Lumen covers well), input monitoring (prompt-injection, adversarial detection -- Lumen has none), output monitoring (hallucination/toxicity/PII/groundedness scoring -- Lumen has none, the single largest missing category), security/compliance (none), embeddings-based anomaly detection (Lumen's Tarjan-SCC is a structurally different, graph-based alternative -- legitimate, not a gap), MELT framework with **OpenTelemetry explicitly named the emerging standard** (validates the otel_* direction even though the fields themselves need the redesign above), RAG metrics (not applicable). **Correctly scoped, not a Lumen defect**: pillars 2-4 (input/output/security) are arguably Prism's job (grading correctness/safety), not Lumen's (which measures efficiency/trajectory) -- a real system-level gap between the two projects, not something to bolt onto Lumen's accumulators. Two industry-wide caveats worth knowing: no established best practice exists yet for alert-threshold tuning (Lumen's unvalidated `SPEC-007` thresholds are in good company, not uniquely bad), and manual review of 50-100 samples remains a best-practice baseline industry-wide -- Lumen has no human-in-the-loop mechanism anywhere.
- **LangSmith evaluation-concepts/observability** (deeper than the eval/insights docs already noted above): vocabulary is `Run` (execution trace, no reference output) / `Example` (inputs + optional reference output) / `Dataset` (collection of Examples) / `Evaluator` (dual-mode: `(example,run)` offline, `(run)` alone online) -- "Trace" itself is used loosely, closer to what Lumen calls `CanonicalTranscript` than a distinct type. Confirms (a second independent time, alongside CodeBurn) that clustering-based session classification, not fixed ratio-thresholds, is the real industry pattern -- LangSmith's own Insights does "unsupervised topic clustering." One point *in Lumen's favor*: LangSmith's anomaly detection is generic ("flag unusual patterns"), no named mechanism -- Lumen's `TrajectoryAnomaly` enum (`CircularLoop`/`ContextFlood`/`GateStall`/`UngroundedDrafting`) is more specific and algorithmically defined.
- **Academic literature** (arXiv, 2026): `RedundancyBench` (arXiv:2605.29893) formalizes exactly what Lumen's Tarjan-SCC cycle detection approximates, with a more rigorous per-step-contribution-labeling methodology to validate against instead of a fixed cycle-depth->=3 threshold. `Graphectory` encodes trajectories as graphs for process-centric (not just outcome) metrics -- same design space as Lumen's `TrajectoryGraph`, worth reading directly. The field has broadly moved to process-level not just outcome-level evaluation (SWE-Bench Pro, SWE Atlas, AgentLens's "Lucky Pass Problem" -- an agent can pass via wrong-reasoning path), validating Prism's `RedGreenGrader`+`TrajectoryGrader` combination directionally. **For Prism's unbuilt `CalibratedJudge`**: a large systematic study (arXiv:2606.19544, 21 judges/9 providers/~541K judgments) found judge rankings shift up to 14 positions across benchmarks, and critically that **high test-retest reliability (>0.95) can coexist with severe position bias (>0.10)** -- a judge can look stable while being systematically biased by anchor ordering -- and that naive exact-match agreement overstates discriminative ability by 33-41 percentage points once bias-corrected. `CalibraEval` (arXiv:2410.15393) is a specific, citable calibration technique. Verdict: the planned "contrastive few-shot anchors" design is on the right track but needs explicit anchor-order randomization and calibration, not just anchors alone, or it will likely reproduce this exact failure mode.

## External research wave, part 3, 2026-08-20 -- comparable open source projects (ccusage, Langfuse, OpenLLMetry, OpenHands)

User asked "what other open source projects are doing something similar." Four parallel forks, each scoped to one project with an explicit "research only, cite real files, don't overstate coverage" instruction (per [[feedback-verify-fork-scope-and-stats]]). All four returned concrete, file-cited findings -- no vague synthesis.

**Convergent lessons -- the same conclusion reached independently by 2-3 unrelated real systems, which is stronger evidence than any single source:**

- **Multi-level/tree-structured agent hierarchy is real, confirmed three independent ways.** Langfuse's `observations` table has a self-referencing nullable `parent_observation_id` (arbitrary depth, not a fixed enum of levels). OpenHands' native `Event` model has an explicit `parent_id` forming a tree, with delegated sub-agents themselves able to delegate further (capped by `max_children`, default 5) -- directly contradicts `CircuitBreakerAccumulator`'s single-level `parent->{agent_type}` string-key model, which structurally cannot represent nesting or multiple distinct children. `ccusage`'s real Claude adapter independently confirms a live top-level `is_sidechain: bool` field on real Claude Code JSONL entries plus subagent transcripts living in sibling files (`<project>/<session>/subagents/<worker>.jsonl`) -- this needs a real redesign, not a patch, and now has three independent reference shapes to design against.
- **Hook telemetry as a first-class separate event/span type, confirmed a second independent way.** OpenHands has a native `HookExecutionEvent` (`hook_event_type: PreToolUse|PostToolUse|UserPromptSubmit|SessionStart|SessionEnd|Stop`, `blocked`, `exit_code`) as its own event class, not embedded in message text -- this is a second, structurally unrelated confirmation (native framework event model, not OTel spans) of the same conclusion the VS Code/Copilot OTel research already reached. Two independent real systems agree: `HookActivityAccumulator` was looking in the wrong place (transcript text) for something that genuinely exists elsewhere as its own event stream, not that it doesn't exist.
- **Cost/pricing data should be a data table (queryable, versioned), not a hardcoded match statement -- confirmed two independent ways, one with a dimension Lumen hasn't considered at all.** Langfuse has real Postgres `Model`/`Price`/`PricingTier` tables joined on `internal_model_id`, plus open `Map(String, ...)` usage/cost fields (not fixed columns) so new token categories need no schema migration. `ccusage`'s Kimi adapter goes further: pricing is **timestamp-gated** -- a hardcoded cutoff switches which model a generic display name (`kimi-for-coding`) resolves to for pricing purposes. Lumen's flat `pricing.rs` match statement needs both a live/queryable-table redesign AND a temporal dimension, not just updated numbers.
- **Pluggable/priority-ordered mapping registries for heterogeneous producers of a nominally-standard format, confirmed real and necessary.** Langfuse's real OTel ingestion (`OtelIngestionProcessor.ts` + `ObservationTypeMapper.ts`) is a priority-ordered registry of `SimpleAttributeMapper`/`CustomAttributeMapper` instances specifically because different SDKs emit `gen_ai.*` spans differently -- direct validation for the pluggable-validator-registry redesign already proposed for `SchemaExtractorAccumulator`. Same underlying problem, independently solved the same way by a mature production system.
- **Idempotent last-write-wins ingestion is the real, proven answer to session-forking/replay double-counting.** Langfuse's ClickHouse tables use `ReplacingMergeTree(event_ts, is_deleted)` specifically for out-of-order/duplicate/updated events -- a concrete, adoptable pattern for the `CodexAdapter` forked-session double-counting risk flagged earlier, not a hypothetical concern to design around from scratch.
- **Malformed-line handling is industry-standard silent-skip, not uniquely a Lumen shortcut -- but that doesn't excuse it.** `ccusage`'s `common/jsonl.rs:61` does exactly what Lumen's `claude.rs:60-66` does (`.ok()`-and-continue on parse failure, no recorded warning). Confirms `CRIT-LUMEN-025`'s overclaim is a real, common gap worth fixing (RTK's `parse_failures` table remains the validated pattern to fix it with), not something to feel uniquely bad about.

**A real, load-bearing spec-vs-shipped-code gap, from reading actual production instrumentation rather than the spec alone:**

- OpenLLMetry's real Anthropic instrumentation (`span_utils.py`) **never sets `gen_ai.conversation.id`** anywhere -- confirms it's aspirational at the provider-instrumentation layer (a raw Anthropic API call has no concept of "conversation" to attach). `gen_ai.response.id` **is** populated in practice, matching spec.
- MCP tool-call spans (`opentelemetry-instrumentation-mcp`) get their own dedicated child span (correct, matches the spec's tool-calls-are-a-separate-span-type model) but populate it with **zero official `gen_ai.tool.*` attributes** -- instead using OpenLLMetry's own proprietary `TRACELOOP_SPAN_KIND`/`TRACELOOP_ENTITY_NAME` vocabulary. A `SpanMappingAccumulator` built strictly against the official registry fields would miss how the most popular real OTel GenAI instrumentation library actually tags the exact span type it's meant to correlate.
- OpenLLMetry's own `MIGRATION.md` documents that even within one vendor's code, exact attribute string values have changed across versions (`gen_ai.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` -> `gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens`; `gen_ai.system` value case changed `"Anthropic"` -> `"anthropic"`) -- concretely validates the registry's own `stability: development` caveat as more than a formality.
- **Implication for the redesign already planned**: build the OTel correlation layer as a tolerant/adapter-pattern consumer (mirroring Langfuse's mapper-registry approach above), not a strict schema match against the official registry -- the registry describes the aspiration, not universally what ships.

**New concrete facts about specific formats, several directly closing previously-open questions:**

Four independent real implementations, four different answers. Its record shape aliases many field names per token count (`input`/`prompt`/`input_tokens`/`prompt_tokens`...), suggesting upstream Gemini CLI's own schema isn't stable either -- this may be a moving target, not a single answer waiting to be found.

## The `~/.gemini/logs/` provenance mystery is now FULLY RESOLVED, 2026-08-20

Root cause: Google discontinued Gemini CLI as a consumer product, replacing it with **Antigravity CLI**, per the official Google Developers Blog (`developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/`, verified directly, not secondhand) -- Antigravity CLI became available to everyone on **2026-05-19**, and Gemini CLI/Gemini Code Assist stopped serving Pro/Ultra and free-tier requests on **2026-06-18** (enterprise-licensed users retain Gemini CLI access). Antigravity spans three real, distinct local products sharing the parent `~/.gemini` namespace, all confirmed present on this machine: `~/.gemini/antigravity/` (the IDE), `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/` (the CLI, aka `agy`), `~/.gemini/antigravity-ide/`. This explains exactly why four independent sources (CodeBurn's two providers, `agent-session-parser`, `ccusage`'s Gemini adapter reading `~/.gemini/tmp/`) all disagreed -- each was written against a different product/era in a fast-moving transition, not this current shape. This machine's session data (dated late July/August 2026) is post-transition, current ground truth.

**The `~/.gemini/logs/*.jsonl` files earlier flagged as "provenance unconfirmed" are literally symlinks**, confirmed via `ls -la`: `~/.gemini/logs/<conversation-id>.jsonl -> ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/<conversation-id>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl`. `logs/` is a convenience flattening layer, not a source of truth in its own right -- adapters should target the `brain/` path.

**Real transcript.jsonl schema, read directly (not inferred)**: one JSON object per line, fields `step_index` (int), `source` (`USER_EXPLICIT` | `MODEL`), `type` (a rich per-action enum: `USER_INPUT`, `LIST_DIRECTORY`, `VIEW_FILE`, `PLANNER_RESPONSE`, others uncatalogued), `status` (`DONE`, others uncatalogued), `created_at` (ISO 8601), `content` (text; for tool-action entries, this is the serialized tool result, not a separate structured result field). `PLANNER_RESPONSE` entries additionally carry `thinking` (reasoning text) and `tool_calls[]` (`name` + `args`, with `args` values themselves JSON-encoded as strings, e.g. `"args":{"DirectoryPath":"\"/Users/gabe/...\""}` -- double-encoded, a real parsing gotcha). This is structurally an Action/Observation-per-type-class model (closer to OpenHands' native model, `type` names the operation, not the message role) -- NOT the `step_index`/`source`/`type` triple in the shape Lumen's existing `AgyAdapter`/`detect_orchestrator` code was built against; the field *names* happen to overlap but the *value vocabulary* was never actually enumerated before now and needs to be checked against the adapter's current match arms.

**Two more real, distinct file shapes for the same conversation, previously unknown:** (1) a sibling `<id>.json` (no `l`) file -- a single JSON object with `sessionId`/`title`/`prompt`/`summary`/`turns[]`, where each turn is `{role, parts: [{text}]}` -- this is the standard Gemini API `Content`/`Part` shape, a precomputed summary/index view, structurally different from the raw `transcript.jsonl` and likely easier to parse if only turn-level (not full tool-call) fidelity is needed. (2) `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/history.jsonl` -- a flat *command-input* history log (`display`, `timestamp` as epoch-millis, `workspace`, `conversationId`, optional `type:"slash_command"`), NOT a conversation transcript -- a third, unrelated artifact type in the same product, useful only for correlating raw user keystrokes/slash-commands to a `conversationId`, not for turn/token reconstruction.

## Pricing architecture decision, 2026-08-20 -- the "exchange rate" model

User proposed, and this is now the settled design direction: **accumulators/adapters should only ever store raw usage data (token counts per category, model name as reported, timestamp) -- never a computed cost.** Cost is derived downstream via a lookup against a **versioned rate table**: rows of `(model, token_type, provider?, rate_per_unit, effective_from, effective_until_nullable)`, looked up by **the turn's own timestamp, not "now"** -- exactly like looking up a historical FX rate for a past transaction, not today's rate. This directly resolves two things found in this research wave, not a novel idea invented in isolation: Langfuse's real schema already separates raw `usage_details`/`cost_details` (open maps) from a separate queryable `Model`/`Price`/`PricingTier` table; `ccusage`'s Kimi adapter already has to do a timestamp-gated cutoff for one specific case (`KIMI_FOR_CODING_K2_6_CUTOFF_MS`) precisely because it lacks a general versioned-rate mechanism and has to hand-code the cutoff instead. This is the general form of that same problem. Practical implications for the redesign: (1) keep any provider-reported cost field (e.g. Claude Code's real `costUSD`) alongside the independently-computed one, not instead of it, mirroring Langfuse's `provided_*`-raw-vs-canonicalized twin-field pattern, so the two can be cross-checked for drift; (2) `pricing.rs`'s fix is this architectural separation, not just refreshed numbers -- the current hardcoded match-statement can't represent a rate change over time at all, which is a real, now-confirmed-necessary case, not a hypothetical one; (3) OpenRouter/LiteLLM's live feeds (already researched) become periodic snapshot sources that insert new `effective_from`-stamped rows, never overwrite old ones -- this is what makes historical cost analysis correct even after a provider changes prices.

## Where real data / reference implementations live (as of 2026-08-20)

- Real Codex CLI sessions: `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl`
- Real OpenCode sessions: `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` (SQLite; `session`/`message`/`part`/`event` tables)
- Real Antigravity CLI sessions (provenance fully resolved -- see dedicated section above): `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/<conversation-id>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl` (raw, real ground truth; `~/.gemini/logs/*.jsonl` are symlinks to this), plus sibling `~/.gemini/logs/<id>.json` (precomputed turn-level summary) and `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/history.jsonl` (unrelated command-input log)
- Real Claude Code sessions (including this very session's own transcript): `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/*.jsonl`
- **CodeBurn** (`github.com/getagentseal/codeburn`, MIT licensed, npm/npx installable): a real, production, multi-orchestrator on-disk session parser covering 37 tools via `src/providers/*.ts` (includes `codex.ts`, `opencode.ts`, `opencode-file-parser.ts`, `antigravity.ts`, `claude.ts`, `kimi.ts`, `kimicode.ts`, `qwen.ts`, `sqlite-session-parser.ts` as a generic SQLite-session factory). Also has `classifier.ts`/`workflow-insights.ts` (real session/turn classification, richer than Lumen's spec'd approach) and `doctor.ts` (validated template for Lumen's unbuilt `DoctorEngine`). Fetch via `gh api repos/getagentseal/codeburn/contents/<path> -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.raw"`.
- **RTK** (`github.com/rtk-ai/rtk`, Apache-2.0, installed locally as `rtk`): a live command-interception proxy, different architecture from Lumen's post-hoc parsing, but its `parse_failures` SQLite table (`~/Library/Application Support/rtk/history.db`) is a validated pattern for durable malformed-input tracking that Lumen's `CRIT-LUMEN-025` claims to do (`"record a warning"`) but doesn't -- confirmed via direct code read that `claude.rs:60-66` just silently `continue`s on a parse error.
- **`ccusage`** (`github.com/ccusage/ccusage`, ~18k stars, hybrid TS/Rust monorepo): the single most directly comparable reference implementation found all session -- same input data AND same language (Rust) as Lumen. Real adapters at `rust/adapters/{claude,codex,opencode,gemini,kimi,qwen,amp,codebuff,copilot,droid,goose,grok,hermes,kilo,openclaw,pi,common}/src/`, shared allocation-conscious JSONL layer at `rust/adapters/common/src/jsonl.rs`. `opencode`'s adapter not yet read (would directly cross-check Lumen's already-verified real OpenCode findings) -- next thing to fetch if resuming this line of research.
- **Langfuse** (`github.com/langfuse/langfuse`, ~33k stars, MIT, YC W23): mature production OSS LLM observability platform. Real data model split across Postgres (`packages/shared/prisma/schema.prisma`, low-volume config) and ClickHouse (`packages/shared/clickhouse/migrations/`, high-volume trace/observation/score event data). Real OTel ingestion at `packages/shared/src/server/otel/{OtelIngestionProcessor,ObservationTypeMapper}.ts`.
- **OpenLLMetry** (`github.com/traceloop/openllmetry`, ~7.4k stars, Apache-2.0): real production OTel GenAI instrumentation. Anthropic instrumentation at `packages/opentelemetry-instrumentation-anthropic/opentelemetry/instrumentation/anthropic/span_utils.py`, MCP tool-span instrumentation at `packages/opentelemetry-instrumentation-mcp/`, migration/versioning history at `packages/opentelemetry-semantic-conventions-ai/MIGRATION.md`. `traceloop-sdk` (higher-level session/workflow wrapping) and the OpenAI/LangChain instrumentation packages not yet read -- open thread on whether `gen_ai.conversation.id` gets set one layer up from where it was checked.
- **OpenHands / `software-agent-sdk`** (`github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk`, Python -- note: the `OpenHands/OpenHands` repo itself is now only the frontend, confirmed via its own `AGENTS.md`, which documents a 5-repo split): the actual agent loop and native event model. `Event`/`Action`/`Observation` hierarchy at `openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/base.py`, delegation at `openhands-tools/.../delegate/impl.py`, stuck-detection at `openhands-sdk/.../conversation/stuck_detector.py`, persistence at `conversation/event_store.py`, compaction at `event/condenser.py`, native hook events at `event/hook_execution.py`. Sibling repos `OpenHands/agent-analysis`, `OpenHands/trajectory-visualizer`, `OpenHands/rubric`, `OpenHands/critic-rubrics`, `OpenHands/ToM-SWE` noticed but not investigated.
- **The real OTel GenAI semantic conventions spec itself**: `github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, attribute definitions at `model/gen-ai/registry.yaml`, span definitions at `model/gen-ai/spans.yaml` -- the opentelemetry.io docs page is only a redirect stub, fetch this repo directly, not the docs site.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/gabe/.claude/plugins/cache/orin-dx-agent-plugins/proof/2.2.0/skills/proof

# proof — Cross-Language Bug-Hunting Skill

## Sub-skills

| Sub-skill | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `proof/scan` | Full hazard sweep across all categories in the workspace |
| `proof/focus` | Targeted scan — caller names one hazard category |
| `proof/verify` | Verify a single reported candidate bug |
| `proof/remediations` | Produce a structured fix plan from a finding-report |

---

## Pipeline

```
workspace → recon → scanner → [boundary-tracer?] → adversary → exit-gate → finding-report@1
```

1. **Recon** — builds verified manifest: live files, dead files, entry points, language.
2. **Scan** — loads language-specific hazard reference, runs grep patterns against live files only, emits candidate@1 list.
3. **Boundary Tracer** *(conditional)* — traces field survival for T7 and T10 candidates. Skipped for all other taxonomies.
4. **Adversary** — reads actual code, traces control flow, and refutes candidates. Batched by crate/module to evaluate multiple candidate signals in one pass, minimizing subagent overhead. Confirms only when a concrete failing scenario can be stated.
5. **Exit Gate** — after remediation, re-reads code from scratch, checks all confirmed findings are gone, scans for sibling gaps, verifies compile and tests. Escalates to human when retry_count exceeds 3.

---

## Dispatch Matrix

| Agent | Mode | Model / Effort | Loads | Input → Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `recon` | Workspace recon | haiku / low | — | workspace path → live/dead manifest + language |
| `scanner` | Pattern matching | sonnet / medium | rust-hazards.md or typescript-hazards.md | manifest → candidate@1 list |
| `boundary-tracer` | Data flow tracing | sonnet / medium | rust-hazards.md or typescript-hazards.md | T7/T10 candidate → field survival map. Conditional. |
| `adversary` | Adversarial reasoning | sonnet / medium | rust-hazards.md or typescript-hazards.md | batched candidate@1 list → finding-report@1 entries or dismissals |
| `exit-gate` | Exit verification | opus / high | — | finding-report@1 → verdict@1 |

---

## Language Detection

Recon inspects the workspace root:
- `Cargo.toml` present → language: `rust` → scanner and adversary load `shared/references/rust-hazards.md`
- `package.json` present → language: `typescript` or `javascript` → scanner and adversary load `shared/references/typescript-hazards.md`

---

## Dead Code Rule

Proof ONLY reports bugs in live, reachable code. Any file not traceable from an entry point is dead and excluded from all scanning and adversarial phases. This is enforced by the recon manifest.

---

## Output

All confirmed findings conform to the `finding-report@1` schema (`shared/schemas/finding-report@1.json`). The exit-gate verdict conforms to `verdict@1` (`shared/schemas/verdict@1.json`).

input.description: Architecture and DX review of Lumen's core crates
input.prompt:
Do NOT re-derive or re-read the session's research memory summaries — you already have that context. Instead, go read the ACTUAL CURRENT CODE right now (it has changed a lot since the memory notes were written) and do a fresh, concrete architecture + DX review.

Scope: crates/lumen-model, crates/lumen-session, crates/lumen-pattern, crates/lumen-analysis, crates/lumen-store, crates/lumen-fixtures in ~/Projects/lumen. Prism (~/Projects/prism) is the real consumer of lumen-model/lumen-session/lumen-pattern (and declares but doesn't yet import lumen-analysis) — review with Prism's-a-real-caller lens in mind, not just Lumen-internal purity.

Cover, with concrete file:line citations for every claim (no vague "could be cleaner" without a specific location):

1. **Semantic modeling correctness** — does the type system honestly represent the domain? Specific things to check: does `PricingTable::rate_for`'s exact-string-match model lookup (added this session) silently produce wrong costs for any real provider-versioned model string that isn't normalized first (e.g. "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022" vs the seeded "claude-3-5-sonnet")? Is there actually a normalization step, or was that assumed but never implemented? Does `CanonicalTranscript` show signs of the "80%-null sparse wide struct" problem (now has otel_conversation_id, service_tier, parse_failures, subagent_role, subagent_role on top of the pre-existing fields — how many of these are None/empty on a typical real session)? Is `OpenCodeAdapter::parse_stream` returning `Err(IngestionError::UnrecognizedFormat)` unconditionally (since its real work moved to `parse_sqlite_session`) a sound trait design, or does it silently break any generic caller that iterates all adapters via the `SessionAdapter` trait expecting `parse_stream` to be the universal entry point? Does `TokenEconomics::calculate` taking `&PricingTable` by reference but every call site constructing a fresh `PricingTable::seed()` per call represent a real, measurable inefficiency (seed() rebuilds a Vec of ~40+ rows on every single adapter parse)?

2. **Architecture** — module boundaries, trait design (`SessionAdapter`), whether the adapter pattern holds up now that OpenCode needs a fundamentally different (random-access file, not BufRead) entry point, whether lumen-analysis's accumulator pattern is consistent across the 6 new accumulators added this session vs the pre-existing ones.

3. **DX for Prism as a real external consumer** — error types (does `IngestionError` give Prism enough to act on?), how ergonomic is constructing a `TurnPricingInput` slice from a real turn stream (does the caller have to do real work lumen-model should be doing?), documentation quality on public API surface, whether the breaking `TokenEconomics::calculate` signature change is discoverable/well-flagged for downstream consumers (changelog? deprecation shim? nothing?).

4. **Anything else structurally concerning** you notice while reading — dead code, inconsistent naming, leaky abstractions.

Rank every finding by severity (blocker / high / medium / low) and be honest if something is actually fine — don't manufacture findings to fill a quota. Report back with a structured list, most severe first. Keep the final report under 200 lines.

Any real session (`"claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"`, `"claude-opus-4-20250514"`, any real GPT-4o/DeepSeek/Kimi date-suffixed string) silently falls into the CRIT-LUMEN-008 "unrecognized model → Sonnet fallback" branch and gets billed at Sonnet rates with **no warning, log, or error** — this is exactly the class of bug the pricing-architecture redesign was supposed to prevent, and it was never wired up. The spec's api_surface lists `ToolCallRepository`, `RollupRepository`, `CommandEventRepository`, `SnapshotRepository`, `TokenUsageRepository` with full method signatures. `ls crates/lumen-store/src/repositories/` → only `findings.rs`, `queue.rs`, `session.rs`, `mod.rs` exist. Grep for any of those five type names in `crates/lumen-store/src/` → zero matches outside the spec JSON itself. The spec text literally says `tool_counts_by_session`/`error_counts_by_session` are "the methods `SessionRepository::get_session` uses... (previously hardcoded to `BTreeMap::new()`)" — but `session.rs:160-161` **still hardcodes `BTreeMap::new()`** for both fields. This is the same "spec certifies fictional code" failure mode the research pass was supposed to eliminate, reintroduced in the very commit meant to fix it.

`fingerprint.rs:7` (tightened this session) requires `sessionId` **AND** `parentUuid`. But `claude.rs:17-19`'s trait-level `matches_fingerprint` still uses the old, looser, untouched condition: `sessionId && (permission-mode || leafUuid || parentUuid)`. TASK-SESSION-001's new negative test (`test_claude_code_fingerprint_sessionid_alone_is_not_claude_code`) only exercises `detect_orchestrator`, never `ClaudeCodeAdapter::matches_fingerprint` — so the two entry points now silently disagree on inputs like `{"sessionId":"x","leafUuid":"y"}` (no `parentUuid`): `detect_orchestrator` says no, `matches_fingerprint` says yes.

**H2. `AgyAdapter`'s `model_family` is permanently hardcoded to a Claude model name — Antigravity/Gemini sessions get Claude Sonnet pricing.**
`agy.rs:45`, never reassigned. Antigravity is a Gemini-lineage orchestrator; there's no seeded Gemini pricing row that could even be matched if the real model string were extracted. Every AGY session's cost is systematically wrong, silently, forever. Pre-existing (not introduced this session), but compounds B1.

**H3. `detect_orchestrator` byte-sniffs via `str::from_utf8` on the raw 2048-byte sample — structurally incompatible with real OpenCode SQLite files, which is the format OpenCode actually ships.**
`fingerprint.rs:5`: `std::str::from_utf8(sample_bytes).unwrap_or("")`. A real SQLite file's header (`"SQLite format 3\0"`) is followed by binary B-tree page bytes almost certain to be invalid UTF-8 within 2048 bytes, so `from_utf8` fails and the whole sample collapses to `""` — `detect_orchestrator` can **never** recognize a real OpenCode `.db` file, full stop. This isn't a future problem: `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` exists on this machine right now and would hit this. TASK-SESSION-005 (the real SQLite fingerprint/parser) is deferred, which is a reasonable scoping call, but the *current* JSONL-based `OpenCodeAdapter::parse_stream` (`opencode.rs:60-207`, still fully live, not stubbed) will happily return `Ok(CanonicalTranscript)` built from a format research confirmed matches no real OpenCode version ever shipped — silent wrong data is worse than a loud failure.

Not yet added (TASK-SESSION-005 deferred), but flagging now since it's a designed-in trap: `SessionAdapter::parse_stream` (`adapter.rs:26-31`) is the trait's only entry point and takes `Box<dyn BufRead>`. A real SQLite parser needs random-access file I/O, so it will have to be a second, non-trait method — meaning `lumen-cli/src/main.rs:64-70`'s `load_session` (which already special-cases each `OrchestratorKind` by hand, not by iterating `Box<dyn SessionAdapter>`) is the only reason this hasn't broken yet. If Prism or any future caller builds a generic adapter registry (`Vec<Box<dyn SessionAdapter>>`) expecting `parse_stream` to be universal, OpenCode will silently never work through it. The trait's abstraction boundary is already cracked before the real implementation even lands.

**M1. `TokenEconomics::calculate` takes `&PricingTable`, but every single call site does `&PricingTable::seed()` inline** — `claude.rs:296`, `agy.rs:183`, `codex.rs:152`, `opencode.rs:202`. `seed()` (`pricing.rs:40-113`) pushes ~40 `PricingRate` rows into a fresh `Vec` on every single adapter parse call. Not yet a measured bottleneck (no benchmark exercises this specific path), but it's a real, avoidable per-parse allocation the `&PricingTable` reference parameter was clearly designed to let callers avoid — nothing hoists it.

**M2. `IngestionError::MalformedJson(String)` is declared but never constructed anywhere** (`adapter.rs:10`; confirmed zero matches in `crates/lumen-session/src/`). Every adapter's real behavior on a malformed line is silent-skip (or, since TASK-SESSION-000/001, push a `ParseFailureRecord` and continue) — never this variant. Dead API surface that misleads a Prism caller pattern-matching on `IngestionError`.

**M3. Zero `///` doc comments on `claude.rs` or `opencode.rs`** (grep count: 0 each), vs. 4-6 in `economics.rs`/`pricing.rs`. The breaking `TokenEconomics::calculate` signature change (5-arg → `&[TurnPricingInput]`) has no changelog, no `#[deprecated]` shim, nothing — a Prism maintainer picking up the new `lumen-model` gets a compile error with no guidance toward `TurnPricingInput`'s existence beyond reading source.

- Accumulator pattern is genuinely consistent: spot-checked `stats.rs` (new, this session) against `flow.rs` (pre-existing) — both follow the same `XMetrics` (Serialize/Deserialize/Default) + `XAccumulator` (`EntryAccumulator` impl) shape. No drift here.
- `CanonicalTranscript`'s field growth (now `otel_conversation_id`, `service_tier`, `parse_failures`, `subagent_role` on top of pre-existing fields) is real but each field is `Option`/empty-collection-safe and semantically justified individually — not yet the "80%-null wide struct" antipattern, more a slow accretion worth revisiting once 2-3 more orchestrator-specific fields land.
- `TokenEconomics::calculate`'s empty-`turns`-slice → zeroed-struct behavior and zero-division guards are correctly implemented and tested (verified in TASK-MODEL-002).

No fabricated findings — B1/B2 alone are severe enough that padding wasn't needed.</result>

## What matters most

The three confirmed code findings share one root cause worth escalating above the individual patches: `CanonicalTurn` lets a turn hold both `tool_calls` and `tool_results`, but no producer ever does, and two consumers assume it does. That is a structural invariant gap — the type permits a state the system never reaches, so correlation logic written against it compiles, passes its tests (`test_accumulators.rs:1447` actually asserts the always-false behavior as if intended), and silently returns constants in production. Fixing `had_error` and `linked_via_vcs_tool` individually will not stop the next accumulator from making the same assumption. That is a `canon`/architect-shaped fix, not a patch.</result>

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

- File: `crates/lumen-model/src/economics.rs`, lines 48-91 (design), with call sites at `crates/lumen-session/src/adapters/claude.rs:284-298`, `codex.rs:140-152`, `opencode.rs:190-199`, and `crates/lumen-session/src/snapshot.rs:26-40`.
- Summary: `calculate()` was redesigned to take `turns: &[TurnPricingInput]` and price each element independently via `rate_for(model, tier, kind, turn.timestamp)` specifically so that "a session whose turns straddle a price-change boundary... is priced correctly on both sides" (its own doc comment) — but every production adapter and `merge_precompact_snapshots` collapses the *entire session's* summed token totals into a single `TurnPricingInput` stamped with only the session's final `ended_at` timestamp before calling it; a grep of the whole workspace (`TokenEconomics::calculate` — 26 call sites, production and test) found not one call site anywhere that passes more than one real element.
- Failure scenario: once `PricingTable` gains a second dated row for a model in active use (exactly the scenario `test_rate_for_versioned_lookup_and_tie_break` already exercises directly against `rate_for`), a real Claude Code session that starts before the rate-effective boundary and ends after it (e.g. spans midnight on the price-change date) will have 100% of its tokens priced at the *single* `ended_at` timestamp's rate — silently overcharging or undercharging the entire session instead of splitting cost across the boundary, with no error raised anywhere.

**2. `ContextGrowthAccumulator` uses `0u64` as both "no previous turn yet" and a legitimate zero prompt-token reading, silently dropping the next real jump**
- File: `crates/lumen-analysis/src/accumulators/context_growth.rs`, line 36 (`update`, lines 29-47).
- Summary: `previous_prompt_tokens: u64` defaults to `0` and the growth guard is `prompt > self.previous_prompt_tokens && self.previous_prompt_tokens > 0`. The struct already uses `Option<u64>` for `initial_prompt_tokens` specifically to avoid this ambiguity, but `previous_prompt_tokens` reuses `0` for both "uninitialized" and "a real turn's prompt_tokens() was exactly 0."
- Failure scenario: three usage-bearing turns with `prompt_tokens()` sequence `[500, 0, 5000]` (a real, if unusual, mid-session turn with zero input/cache tokens sandwiched between two normal turns). After turn 2, `previous_prompt_tokens` becomes `0`. On turn 3, `5000 > 0` is true but `self.previous_prompt_tokens > 0` is false, so the genuine 5000-token jump is *not* recorded: `total_growth` stays `0` and `max_jump_tokens` stays `0` instead of `5000`, and `avg_growth_per_turn` reports `0.0` instead of reflecting real context growth. The existing test (`test_context_growth_skips_missing_usage_and_zero_growth_floor`) covers the "first-turn" zero case and the "no-usage-turn interleaved" case but never a real zero-valued usage-bearing turn, so this is untested.

**3. OpenCode adapter drops cache-write/cache-read tokens whenever a usage object reports zero fresh input/output tokens**
- File: `crates/lumen-session/src/adapters/opencode.rs`, lines 87-98 (inside `parse_stream`, guard at line 87).
- Summary: `in_tok`, `out_tok`, `c_write`, `c_read` are all read unconditionally from the same `metrics`/`usage` object, but accumulation into `current_cache_write`/`current_cache_read` (and `turn_usage`) is gated behind `if in_tok > 0 || out_tok > 0` — a condition that only inspects two of the four fields. This is a distinct bug from the already-confirmed `accumulated_cost`-shadows-`input_tokens` issue (bug #7); it's the surrounding gate, not the field-selection chain.
- Failure scenario: a line whose `metrics` object is `{"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0,"cache_read_input_tokens":5000}` (a pure cache-hit step with no fresh generation) is silently dropped in its entirety — `current_cache_read` never increases, `turn_usage` stays `None` — even though a real cache read occurred, undercounting `cache_hit_ratio` and `total_cost_usd` for the session.

**4. `TokenUsageAccumulator::finalize()` discards its own correctly-tracked per-model breakdown and never computes per-model cost**
- File: `crates/lumen-analysis/src/accumulators/token_usage.rs`, `update_raw` lines 27-61 (builds `self.per_model`) vs. `finalize` lines 64-80 (never reads it).
- Summary: `update_raw` correctly builds `self.per_model: HashMap<CompactString, ModelTokenSummary>` keyed by each message's *actual* `model` field, incrementing `input_tokens`/`output_tokens`/`cache_creation_tokens`/`cache_read_tokens`/`turns` per real model — but never increments `entry.cost_usd` (permanently `0.0`). `finalize()` then ignores `self.per_model` entirely and calls `TokenEconomics::calculate()` with only the grand-total counters and `self.default_model`, which reconstructs a *different*, single-entry `per_model` map keyed solely by `default_model`.
- Failure scenario: a session with messages from two real (non-synthetic) models, e.g. `claude-3-5-haiku-20241022` and `claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022`, constructed via `TokenUsageAccumulator::new("claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022")`. The output `TokenEconomics.per_model` has exactly one entry keyed `"claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"` containing the *combined* totals of both models — the Haiku usage is silently mis-attributed to Sonnet in any per-model cost breakdown, and the accumulator's own correctly-split `self.per_model` data is thrown away. The existing test (`test_accumulators.rs:534-566`) only ever feeds one real model, so this mis-attribution is untested.

All four were checked against the confirmed-defects list and are mechanically distinct from every item on it (verified each by re-reading the exact cited lines of items 1-15 and confirming none overlaps). No off-by-one column-index bugs were found in `lumen-store`'s repositories (I cross-checked every `SELECT`'s column list against every `row.get(N)` mapping in `session.rs`, `queue.rs`, and `findings.rs` — all correctly aligned), and the previously-suspected `source_hash: u64 as i64` cast is safe (Rust's `as` between same-width integer types is a lossless bit-reinterpretation, confirmed round-trips for the full `u64` range). The `StatsAccumulator` byte-vs-char-count pattern I initially flagged turned out to be explicitly intentional and already tested (`test_stats_mutually_exclusive_roles_and_byte_length`), so it is correctly excluded.</result>

Adversarial review — crates/lumen-model, lumen-session, lumen-pattern, lumen-analysis, lumen-store

Ledger Audit

Six independent review passes — bug hunt, security, spec-drift verification, architecture, and simplification — run against this session's 22 commits. The short version: the test suite is green, and the pricing engine is wrong for almost every real session.

5
Blocker
9
High
11
Medium
0
Security vulns
60
Files scanned
96/96
Tests passing

The headline

Every dollar figure is suspect

PricingTable::rate_for matches model names by exact string equality. No adapter normalizes a raw provider string (claude-opus-4-20250514, gemini-2.0-flash-001) to the short seeded key (claude-opus, gemini-2.0-flash) before calling it. Every one of those misses falls through the "unrecognized model" guard and gets billed at Claude 3.5 Sonnet's rate — silently, with no warning or log line.

This was verified by direct execution, not inference: rate_for("claude-3-5-haiku-20241022", ...), rate_for("claude-opus-4-20250514", ...), rate_for("gpt-4o-2024-08-06", ...), and rate_for("gemini-2.0-flash-001", ...) all return Sonnet's $3.00 / $3.75 / $0.30 / $15.00 per-M rates. Claude 3.5 Sonnet is the only model priced correctly today, and only by coincidence — it's the fallback target.

A second, independent bug compounds it: any Codex session that reports a service_tier (the fixture itself carries one) prices the entire session at $0.00, because the pricing table has no tiered rows and the tier filter simply finds nothing to match.

Blocker

5 findings

Wrong output with no visible failure. Each of these passes the current test suite.

Blockercrates/lumen-model/src/pricing.rs:118–135
No model-string normalization anywhere in the workspace

Confirmed by canon:drift-checker against every provider criterion: 9 of 20 pricing acceptance criteria are drifted, all from this one root cause. claude.rs passes the raw message.model field straight through; agy.rs, codex.rs, and opencode.rs never reassign model_family from its hardcoded default at all.

Trigger & fix

Trigger: ingest any real session from any of the four adapters. Real model strings carry date suffixes or provider prefixes the seed table's short keys don't.

Fix: add a normalization step in rate_for (or immediately before calling it) that strips known version suffixes to the canonical key — the spec's own PricingTable api_surface entry already promises this behavior, it was just never implemented.

Blockercrates/lumen-model/src/pricing.rs:134 · codex.rs:148
Any Codex service_tier zeroes the entire session's cost

PricingTable::seed() pushes every row with tier: None. When a Codex payload sets tier: Some("Standard"), the tier-equality filter matches zero rows for all four rate kinds, and unwrap_or(0.0) silently returns $0.00. The test suite's own comment documents the harness as "NOT IMPLEMENTED" and names live violations already present (a per-turn BTreeMap collect in pr_link.rs, a format! allocation in circuit_breaker.rs). Two stated invariants are in direct tension.

Mediumcrates/lumen-model/src/economics.rs:123
1-hour cache tier is permanently zero, and the discount ratio it's supposed to encode isn't consistent

ephemeral_1h_tokens is hardcoded to 0 — no signal populates it anywhere. AGENTS.md's "deterministic token accounting" invariant implies a single cache-read discount ratio; the seed table actually varies it per model (0.10× for Anthropic, 0.25× for Gemini Flash, 0.14× for GLM), which the invariant's wording doesn't account for.

Mediumclaude.rs:295 · agy.rs:183 · codex.rs:152 · opencode.rs:202
A fresh PricingTable is allocated on every single parse call

TokenEconomics::calculate takes &PricingTable specifically so callers can reuse one — every real call site instead does &PricingTable::seed() inline, rebuilding a ~40-row Vec on every adapter invocation. Not yet measured as a bottleneck, but a real, avoidable allocation the API was designed to let callers skip.

Mediumcrates/lumen-session/src/adapter.rs:10
Dead API surface that misleads callers

IngestionError::MalformedJson(String) is declared but constructed nowhere. Every adapter's real behavior on a bad line is silent-skip or, since this session, a ParseFailureRecord — never this variant. A caller pattern-matching on IngestionError will write dead-code branches for it.

Mediumcrates/lumen-model — TokenEconomics::calculate signature change
The breaking pricing API change has no migration note

claude.rs and opencode.rs carry zero /// doc comments. The 5-argument → per-turn-slice signature change has no changelog entry, no deprecation shim, nothing pointing a downstream maintainer toward TurnPricingInput. This is exactly the change that will break Prism's build the moment it updates — see the note below.

Mediumcrates/lumen-analysis/src/engine.rs:121–125
The full accumulator pipeline runs per subagent to keep one field

Every subagent transcript runs the complete recursive process_transcript — all 19 accumulators — and only .attribution survives into by_subagent. The type signature makes this an intentional narrowing, not silent data loss, but it's real computational waste at recursion depth, worth revisiting if subagent-heavy sessions become common.

Mediumcrates/lumen-session/src/adapters/codex.rs:144–145
Codex cache tokens are hardcoded to zero

cache_creation_tokens/cache_read_tokens are always 0 in Codex's TurnPricingInput — no cache-related key is ever probed in the token_count payload. Unresolved: no real Codex session fixture exists in the repo to confirm whether Codex's actual wire format even carries cache-token data, so this may be dead code rather than data loss — flagged as an open question, not a confirmed bug.

Mediumcrates/lumen-session/src/adapters/claude.rs:109
Open question: is_sidechain may not match real Claude Code's field name

The sidechain-exclusion filter reads is_sidechain (snake_case); every fixture in the repo uses that spelling too — but no fixture in this codebase has been checked against a real, live Claude Code JSONL export. If the real field is isSidechain (camelCase), CRIT-LUMEN-026's entire subagent-exclusion mechanism never fires in production, silently contaminating the main transcript with subagent turns. Worth a direct check against ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl before trusting this either way.

Test coverage

Direct answer to "are we covering the happy path and the edge cases": no — not as thoroughly as 96/96 green suggests. canon:drift-checker re-read both specs from disk and empirically probed each criterion's exact condition rather than trusting the tests' own framing.

pricing & economics

SPEC-LUMEN-002-SESSION

11 / 15 6 / 15 3 genuine divergences, 3 correct-but-unproven-by-test.

Codex's cumulative-token test (CRIT-LUMEN-110) uses exactly two ascending readings — max() would pass identically to the correct last-write logic; it was never exercised with a third, descending line, the one input that would discriminate. The CLI never actually calls lumen-store or lumen-analysis

Both crates are declared Cargo.toml dependencies of lumen-cli; main.rs imports neither. Published. Here's the summary while `code-review` finishes in the background — I'll fold its findings in when it lands.

## The headline

**The pricing engine is wrong for almost every real session, and the test suite can't see it.** `PricingTable::rate_for` matches model names by exact string equality with zero normalization anywhere in the workspace. Real provider strings like `"claude-opus-4-20250514"` or `"gemini-2.0-flash-001"` all silently fall through to Claude 3.5 Sonnet's rate — verified by direct execution, not inference. Separately, any Codex session reporting a `service_tier` prices the **entire session at $0.00**, because no tiered rate rows exist.

## What else turned up

- **5 blockers, 9 high, 11 medium** findings across bugs, spec-drift, and architecture — full detail in the artifact
- **Security: clean** — zero high-confidence vulnerabilities
- **A structural gap, not a local bug**: `CanonicalTurn` allows a turn to hold both `tool_calls` and `tool_results`, but no adapter ever produces that shape — two accumulators built assuming otherwise silently produce constant wrong output, and a test asserts the broken behavior as correct
- **`lumen-cli` silently fakes success** on any unrecognized session file — falls back to the Claude parser, which can't fail on wrong-schema input, and exits 0 with a fabricated $0.00 report
- **Test coverage**: SPEC-001 (pricing) is 11/20 criteria genuinely covered, 9/20 drifted. SPEC-002 (adapters) is 11/15 covered, 6/15 drifted — three of those are cases where the code is actually correct but the test can't tell correct from broken (e.g. Codex's cumulative-token test only has ascending values, so `max()` would pass identically to the right last-write logic)
- **Open question worth checking**: `is_sidechain` (snake_case) was never verified against a real Claude Code export — if the real field is `isSidechain`, the whole subagent-exclusion mechanism never fires in production

## Agent-plugins

Five of nine toolkits used (`proof`, `security-review`, `code-review`, `canon:drift-checker`, general fork); the other four (`axiom`, `canon`/`vector`, `trace`, `delta`/`graph`) are legitimate non-fits for reviewing already-committed code, not an oversight — detailed in the artifact.

Nothing's been fixed yet — this is findings only. Given the scale, want to talk through priority before I start applying fixes, or should I just start from the top (pricing normalization first, since it's the one bug touching every dollar figure the system produces)?
